lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the price system
lead.head: You can’t outlaw gravity
body: Amit Varma opened with a grievance against gravity, which makes Bengalis slouch. The state, he proposed, should use its coercive power to outlaw it.
Ajay Shah had a counter-offer: “Or I can write the gorgeous economics book, *Floating to Utopia*.” {066-J01}

The joke had a point. Supply and demand, Varma said, is a law of economics much like gravity. “You can no more make society better by messing with prices than you can make us fly by creating a law against gravity.”

Over the next hour the hosts took apart five ways governments meddle with prices: price caps, rent control, the minimum wage, minimum support prices for crops and import tariffs. Each time, they argued, it is the poor who pay.
## A miracle nobody planned

The case starts with Friedrich Hayek’s essay *The Use of Knowledge in Society*, written in the mid-1940s against the central planners. Society, Hayek argued, is too complex, and wants change too fast, for anyone to plan it from the top.

“How do people like you and me fulfil the needs of people millions of miles away who we don’t know, we will never meet, and yet we play a part in their happiness?” Varma asked. “And the answer is prices.” {066-C01}

Prices carry information and incentives at once, Varma said. If a fire consumed a tenth of India’s timber, he would learn of it from dearer pencils and furniture, and economise, while growers would be drawn in.
## Five ways to break it
Cap the price of a car at Rs 10,000, Varma said, and cars do not become affordable. They vanish into shortages, queues and black markets.
Rent control, he said, is one reason buildings on Bombay’s Marine Drive are dilapidated, with some tenants paying around Rs 150 a month for flats that would otherwise fetch four or five lakh.

A minimum wage prices out anyone whose work is worth less than the floor. In India, Shah said, it is about Rs 13,000, against Rs 8,000 across the border in Bangladesh, and India has one of the lowest employment rates in the world. {#wage}
Support prices tilted farmers towards cereals and, in arid Punjab, towards rice, whose burnt stubble fouls Delhi’s air every year.

And a tariff quietly takes a few rupees from every consumer and hands them to an organised lobby. Hence Varma’s Law: “Every interference in free markets leads to a redistribution of wealth from the poor to the rich.” {066-C13}
## The lesson that fades
Shah held up Europe as the model. When Putin cut off its gas, nobody capped the price. Supply surged, and governments paid poor households directly so they could afford the expensive gas.
So why do politicians keep reaching for caps? Varma counted both Kamala Harris and Donald Trump, in the current US election, among the enemies of the price system.
Shah called the forgetting a sorcerer’s apprentice problem: people raised in prosperity know that the system works but not why, and slip back into the instinct that the government should fix things.

Political maturity, Shah said, is the ability to stomach large price fluctuations. “Wisdom lies in creating a world of freedom where prices fluctuate and then being quiet and doing nothing using state power when prices go up or prices go down.” {066-C08}

second.label: Cement and steel
second.head: A ministry in mourning
second.deck: Ajay Shah’s journalist friend watched officials grieve when price controls ended
body: In the early 1980s a journalist friend of Ajay Shah’s covered the cement and steel ministries, just as the government abolished its price controls on both.

Under the controls, Shah said, anyone who wanted to build had to battle for cement and steel, or ended up with substandard cement. He draws a direct line from it to buildings of the 1950s and 1960s that later collapsed.

When decontrol was announced, the whole government building felt a personal catastrophe: the market would now sort out cement and steel, and nobody needed the officials any more. {066-S01} As Shah put it, “in a sensible country you don’t need a ministry of steel, you don’t need a ministry of cement.” {#ministry}

quote.text: They had this aura of a catastrophe like some family member has died.

second.caption: the ministry that mourned decontrol

third.head: Capped fare, missed flight
body: Delhi once tried capping Uber’s surge pricing, Amit Varma said. A friend of his who knows economics well didn’t know about the cap, did not plan for the shortage, and missed his flight. {066-S03}
Varma’s thought experiment: 200 cabs serve 200 riders, then supply falls to 100. {#ubers} With surge pricing, the rider rushing to a hospital or an airport can outbid someone going out casually.

The surge also reaches the idle driver. “You are sitting at a katta. Maybe if you’re Bengali, you’re going to have an afternoon nap at that point,” Varma said. Seeing double the fare, he joins the supply. {066-J06}
In the long run, an apprentice carpenter might become a driver. Cap the fare and all three effects switch off: the cabs go first come, first served.
third.caption: the friend who missed his flight

p2.title: The price is right
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the miracle of prices, and the many ways the state spoils it

sections.label: The foundation
sections.head: No committee made this pencil
sections.caption: the miracle of prices
body: Friedrich Hayek wrote *The Use of Knowledge in Society* in the mid-1940s, Amit Varma said, as a reply to central planners who believed they could decide from the top how much of every good to make and what it should cost. Hayek later called that belief the fatal conceit. {066-R03}

Hayek’s answer was that the world is too complex. Millions of people “contain multitudes”, Varma said, and their wants change from minute to minute. Only a decentralised system can cope, and that system has existed forever: prices.

Leonard Read’s essay *I, Pencil* shows the miracle at work. A pencil comes out of the cooperation of people in forty countries, felling timber, shipping it, fitting the graphite, with no genius and no committee in charge. {#pencil}
## The resource allocation

Ajay Shah, admitting that economists are “very bad people” who turn ordinary words into jargon, called the whole arrangement the resource allocation: a complete list of who must do what in an economy. {066-J05}

Written down, Shah said, it would run to millions of pages. Central planning tries to write it, as Indian finance still does through tens of thousands of pages of regulation. Markets discover it instead.
~ “The only thing that crosses the cell wall of the firm is the price,” he said. “And all the magic of the market economy happens.” {066-C02}

quote.text: Prices act as both information and they act as incentives.

sections.label: Price caps
sections.head: Cheap cars, none for sale
sections.caption: price caps
body: Imagine, Amit Varma said, that a leader decides everyone should own a car, and caps the price at Rs 10,000. {#cars}
Ajay Shah asked listeners to pause on the horror of it: a law that uses state coercion to penalise a transaction between consenting adults at any other price.

The consequences follow at once, Varma said. Cars stop selling, and what stock exists goes to the black market or to whoever comes first. The cap does not make cars cheaper; it takes them out of existence. {066-C04}
## The usual something

Caps on air tickets after a natural disaster, perhaps the Kerala floods, conjure no new planes, he said. The seats go first come, first served, so a passenger with a dire emergency may get nothing while a trivial trip goes ahead.
Nixon’s gasoline cap in the 1970s OPEC crisis brought long queues at gas stations. Venezuelans paid black-market prices for toilet paper and milk. Soviet bread lines went around blocks.
Why do politicians keep at it? Varma quoted *Yes Minister*: “this is a problem, we must do something, this is something, let’s do it.” The usual something is a price cap. {066-J13}
~ In a competitive market, Varma said, everything is priced the way it is for a reason, and a fat profit margin draws in newcomers until it sorts itself out.

quote.text: You haven’t actually made a change in the price of the thing. You’ve just taken it out of existence.

sections.label: Rent control
sections.head: Rent asunder
sections.caption: rent control
body: Amit Varma reached rent control by way of a mondegreen. For years he heard ‘Aabodana’, in a song from the 1970s film *Gharaonda* about being alone in the city in search of shelter, as ‘Sabudana’. {066-J08}

A government sees voters struggling with rising rents and fixes the rent, so the landlord cannot raise it. “The intention is good and that is seen,” Varma said. “The consequence is bad and that is unseen.” {066-C09}

Landlords stop maintaining their buildings. Developers stop building. Housing grows scarce, so everything outside rent control costs more. Over the years the property’s value falls towards nothing, which for the owner is theft.
## Where you sit

Varma and Ajay Shah both know a leftist, a hardcore statist, who has lived for two generations in a rent-controlled flat near Shivaji Park. Where you stand depends on where you sit, Varma said. {066-S06}

In an early episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, the economist Alex Tabarrok told Varma that the rent-controlled parts of New York looked like a bombed-out city. Varma recalled the dystopian film *Escape from New York*. {066-J15}
~ He also pointed to Michael Shellenberger’s *San Fransicko*, and to Hernando de Soto’s *The Mystery of Capital*: a property drained of its value by the state stops working as capital. {066-R14}

quote.text: He has been a lifelong beneficiary of theft enabled by the state.

sections.label: Minimum wage
sections.head: Priced out of a job
sections.caption: the minimum wage
body: Amit Varma once believed a minimum wage was how you pull a country out of poverty. A Milton Friedman video changed his mind and sent him down a rabbit hole of books and articles. {066-R15}

The logic is simple, he said. Fix the minimum at 100 and anyone whose work the market values at 90 is priced out of a job. Thomas Leonard’s *Illiberal Reformers* shows that some progressive labour laws of the first half of the twentieth century were meant to keep African Americans and women out of work.
## Both sides at once

In India, Ajay Shah said, the minimum wage is about Rs 13,000, while in comparable Bangladesh the wage is Rs 8,000. Mandatory entitlements push the cost of hiring at the lowest levels to about Rs 17,000 a month. {#allin}

The same number feeds NREGS payments, which anchor what workers expect. So firms are kept from hiring and workers from accepting, and India ends up with one of the world’s lowest employment rates, below Bangladesh, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia.
Bangladesh, meanwhile, rides a labour-intensive manufacturing boom: those earning 8,000 yesterday earn 10,000 today, Varma said, and will earn 13,000 tomorrow.
~ Shah backed KP Krishnan’s idea for breaking the logjam: free IT and IT-enabled services from labour law first, then extend it to other industries if it works. {066-R18}

quote.text: The alternative to a low wage job is not a high wage job. The alternative to a low wage job is no job.

sections.label: Import tariffs
sections.head: Ten rupees you never see
sections.caption: import tariffs
body: A local maker sells something for Rs 100, Amit Varma said. A Chinese seller offers the same quality for Rs 90. {#china}
The local makers lobby, and the government puts a tariff of Rs 20 on the Chinese good, which now costs Rs 110. The consumer buys local for Rs 100, paying Rs 10 more without even knowing it.

Those ten rupees, from every dispersed consumer, would have gone into the economy and created jobs. That is unseen. What is seen is the local maker doing well. Gathered together, the rupees go to an interest group: Varma’s Law in action. {066-C13}
## A game nobody lifts

Protection hurts the firm too, Varma said. Shielded from China on price and quality, it need not lift its game. Exposed to the world, it would build better processes, the learning would seep into the economy, and it might even export. {066-C14}
Ajay Shah added that transport, by container ship or by air, already protects domestic firms: getting goods to Bombay is easier from Pune than from Mozambique.
~ Varma, by his own account, hates tariffs, and said so impolitely. “If I’m trading with someone in China and we are having a double thank you moment, what the F is anyone’s problem?” he asked.

quote.text: Now the more competition there is, the more we have to lift our game, the harder we have to try

sections.label: Why we forget
sections.head: The sorcerer’s apprentices
sections.caption: generational amnesia
body: If people learn from their mistakes, Amit Varma asked, why hasn’t politics learnt its lessons? In the current US election, he said, Kamala Harris, with her talk of price gouging, and Donald Trump are both enemies of the price system. {066-J19}
Ajay Shah recalled Angela Merkel’s line: Germany’s future would be known only when generations with no memory of the Second World War came of age and formed their own political philosophy.

Economics, he said, has the same problem. Hayek, Friedman and others won the argument, and a great age of prosperity followed, but those raised in it lost the connection with where they came from. {066-C15}
## Fall, diagnose, repeat

His working hypothesis is that every ten, twenty or thirty years, governments must try activism and fall flat, and there must be enough intellectualism around to diagnose the failure. Pensions show the danger: twenty-five years on, the lessons have not been learnt. {#pensions}

Varma met the same amnesia at a conference on liberalism in Washington, DC. Azar Nafisi, author of *Reading Lolita in Tehran*, said liberal values are voiced most truly by dissenters in Iran, for whom it is an existential battle. {066-S09}
~ Someone born in 2004, Varma said, never saw pre-liberalisation India or the Soviet Union. Hence his warning: “the price of liberty has to be eternal vigilance.” {066-J21}

quote.text: So it’s like a sorcerer’s apprentice problem that this thing works, but you don’t know why it works.

side.boxText: Friedrich Hayek’s *The Use of Knowledge in Society*, written in the mid-1940s against the central planners, argues that knowledge is too dispersed for anyone to plan from the top. Amit Varma says he still often thinks of it, to remind himself. {066-R02}

contQuote.text: There is a furnace that makes prosperity, which is the market economy. And then a government may choose to tax that market economy and use it for helping poor people through direct transfers, but you don’t interfere with the furnace.

p3.title: Price tales
p3.deck: Four stories of prices left alone, and prices meddled with

stories.start: I want to talk about a story from Twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-three
stories.end: one of the most perfect stories of how to do public policy
stories.caption: Europe’s gas crisis
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Putin’s energy blackmail and Europe’s reply
stories.head: The squeeze that prices broke
body: When Putin invaded Ukraine, Ajay Shah said, he also tried energy blackmail. Europe had imprudently come to rely on Russian gas, and Putin hoped that by cutting the supply he could break the Western coalition backing Ukraine.
The price of gas went “up to infinity”, Shah said. {#infinity} Russian propaganda talked openly of Europeans freezing to death in their houses and coming back to beg.

Yet nobody in the European policy space reached for price controls. {066-S04} On the demand side, the high price sorted users out: some factories shut down, some switched to electricity, and some paid up and kept running.

On the supply side, engineering companies built new LNG terminals in no time. European buyers scoured the world and diverted tankers out of Qatar that were bound for other countries. And in the United States, where fracking and horizontal drilling had already made the shale revolution, gas production and exports surged.
“The supply response only comes in response to the price,” Shah said. Interfere with a high price, and you interfere with the supply response.

That left the poor. Governments knew that pro-Putin far-right parties could win over voters freezing at home, so they made large on-budget payments to poor people, who used them to buy the expensive gas.

~ Nobody had expected Europe to beat the blackmail. For Shah it was “one of the most perfect stories of how to do public policy”. Amit Varma marvelled that no committee of Europe’s most important people could have planned it: “all these solutions came from unexpected places.”

quote.text: And I was fascinated and impressed that nobody but nobody in the European policy space jumped to price controls as the answer.

stories.postscript: Pranay Kotasthane and Nitin Pai had voiced exactly this fear on *The Seen and the Unseen* when the war broke out, Varma recalled.

stories.start: When I was in college, there was an earthquake in an interior part
stories.end: But when you interfere with prices, it just creates a huge problem
stories.caption: the grocery store after the earthquake
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s bleeding-heart moment in a quake zone
stories.head: The last shop standing
body: As a college student, Amit Varma spent three days in an ambulance with paramedic friends, driving through the earthquake-hit parts of Maharashtra, Latur among them.

In one village, one side had fallen down entirely. On the other stood a single grocery store, and villagers complained that it was charging so much it should be outlawed. “And my initial thought was how dare they, these evil capitalists,” Varma said. “I used to read Marx in those days.” {066-S02}

Today he would let the price system work. High prices make it likelier that supplies reach the village, and that households economise: half a packet of bread instead of three, shared with the neighbour, the cost split.
~ In an emergency, he said, the government should spend its own money on those affected by a disaster. Interfering with prices only creates a huge problem.
stories.why: A high price in a disaster is a signal that pulls in supply and stretches what is left. Compassion, in Varma’s telling, belongs in the government’s own spending, not in caps. Letting prices adjust in real time, he said, is miraculous. {066-C06}

stories.start: For example, Punjab is an added state. Punjab should not grow rice
stories.end: who are benefiting from it will fight back tooth and nail
stories.caption: Punjab’s rice and Delhi’s smog
stories.kicker: Amit Varma traces Delhi’s smog to a price in Punjab
stories.head: Rice in Punjab, smoke in Delhi
body: Punjab is arid, Amit Varma said, and should not grow rice, which needs a lot of water. But the government announced a minimum support price for rice. {066-S08}

So farmers used free farm electricity, which mainly benefits rich farmers, to dig borewells and pump out ever more water. After the harvest comes rice stubble, and the cheapest way to be rid of it is to burn it.
“Every year at that particular time of the year when the farmers of Punjab burn their rice stubble, a foul wind carries it to Delhi,” Varma said, and the city’s pollution is then at its worst.
~ There is no political solution, he said. The same party rules both states, but nobody can mess with the farmers, who will fight back tooth and nail.
stories.why: One distorted price set off a chain: depleted groundwater, burnt fields, foul air and political deadlock. A price intervention, Varma said, builds an equilibrium that is extremely difficult to break out of, because those who benefit fight back.
stories.postscript: Support prices for cereals but not pulses, Varma recalled, meant more carbohydrates and less protein in India: “a humanitarian crime”. {066-S07}

stories.start: If you walk the streets of Marine Drive in Bombay, for example
stories.end: where the flats would actually be like four lakhs, five lakhs a month
stories.caption: Marine Drive’s rent-controlled flats
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on rent control in Bombay
stories.head: Marine Drive, ₹150 a month
body: Walk along Marine Drive in Bombay, Amit Varma said, and you will often find buildings that are old, dilapidated and not in great shape. He points to rent control, which India started in 1949, as one reason. {#rent-1949}
He hears of tenants paying “ridiculous amounts like Rupees one fifty a month or whatever”, for flats that would otherwise rent for four or five lakh a month. {066-S05}

At such rents a landlord has no reason to maintain the building, and no developer has reason to build. “Would you build a building in Marine Drive if your rent is going to be one fifty rupees or whatever the hell it is?” Varma asked.
~ Housing grows scarce, and everything outside rent control costs more. These are not even unintended consequences, Varma said: economic theory predicts exactly this.
stories.why: A tenant’s cheap rent is the seen benefit; a crumbling building, no new construction and dearer flats for everyone else are the unseen cost. For the landlord, Varma said, rent control is theft. {066-C09}

quiz.q: What did Amit Varma propose the state should outlaw, so that Bengalis would stop slouching?
quiz.a: Gravity, with an application for the ban to be written in triplicate.

quiz.q: What, according to Varma’s Law, does every interference in free markets lead to?
quiz.a: A redistribution of wealth from the poor to the rich, said Varma.

quiz.q: How did the cement and steel ministries react when price controls on both were abolished?
quiz.a: As if a family member had died: their importance was knocked out.

quiz.q: Why did a friend of Varma’s, who knows his economics, miss a flight in Delhi?
quiz.a: Uber surge pricing had been capped, and he didn’t know about it.

quiz.q: According to Ajay Shah, what is the alternative to a low-wage job?
quiz.a: Not a high-wage job, Shah said, but no job at all.

quiz.q: Where, according to Azar Nafisi, are classical liberal values expressed in their truest sense?
quiz.a: Among dissenters in Iran, for whom it is an existential battle.
